title: Set up SSH for git
tagline: Keys, agent and config, so pushing stops asking who you are.
intro: One key per machine, added to the agent once, pasted into GitHub once. After that git never asks for a password.

sections.title: Overview
sections.summary: Five steps, then it is done for good.

blocks.caption: Where the key goes and who checks it.

items.label: Create the key
items.detail: ssh-keygen writes two files: the secret half, and the .pub half you may share
explain: ssh-keygen -t ed25519 writes id_ed25519 and id_ed25519.pub side by side in ~/.ssh. The comment is only a label, so put the machine's name in it rather than yours.
The passphrase encrypts the private key on disk, which is what makes a stolen laptop harmless; the agent is what saves you from typing it all day.
Ed25519 over RSA: shorter, faster, and accepted by GitHub everywhere. Reach for RSA only when some older server refuses it.

items.label: ssh-agent
items.detail: Keeps the key unlocked in memory, so git never stops to ask for the passphrase
explain: ssh-add hands the unlocked key to a process that holds it in memory, so the passphrase is asked once per login instead of once per push.
On macOS, --apple-use-keychain saves the passphrase in the Keychain, and the key is back in the agent by itself after a restart.
ssh-add -l lists what the agent is holding. An empty list is the usual reason git has suddenly started asking for a password again.

items.label: GitHub
items.detail: Paste only the .pub half. GitHub uses it to recognise you and never needs the secret one
explain: Settings → SSH and GPG keys → New SSH key, then paste the whole .pub file including the ssh-ed25519 prefix and the trailing comment.
GitHub only ever sees the public half. It proves you hold the private one by asking you to sign a challenge, never by receiving the key itself.
One public key cannot sit on two GitHub accounts — the second upload is refused, and that single rule is what forces the two-key setup below.

items.label: Test
items.detail: ssh -T greets you by name once the agent and GitHub hold the matching halves
explain: ssh -T git@github.com answers with your username and says shell access is not provided. That message is the success case, not an error.
ssh -vT git@github.com prints which key files were offered and in what order — the fastest way to find out the agent is answering with the wrong one.

items.label: SSH remote
items.detail: A repo cloned over HTTPS keeps asking for a token until its remote url is switched
explain: git remote set-url origin git@github.com:owner/repo.git switches an existing clone over; nothing else in the repository changes.
git remote -v is the check. A url that still starts with https:// goes through a token no matter how well the key is set up.

Load it into ssh-agent and the macOS keychain
Paste the .pub half into GitHub

sections.title: Create the key
sections.summary: Two files: one secret, one public.

items: ed25519, not RSA — shorter, faster, and what GitHub recommends.
Set a passphrase. The keychain remembers it, so you type it once.
One key per machine. Do not copy a private key between computers.
id_ed25519 is the secret half; id_ed25519.pub is the half you share.

blocks.caption: Generate it, named after the machine

sections.title: Load it into the agent
sections.summary: The agent holds the unlocked key so git can use it silently.

items: --apple-use-keychain stores the passphrase in the macOS keychain.
The config file re-adds the key after every reboot.
On Linux, drop the apple flags and let the desktop keyring hold it.
Copy the public key to the clipboard.
GitHub → Settings → SSH and GPG keys → New SSH key.
Title it after the machine, paste, and save.

body: Only the .pub file ever leaves the machine. If you paste the file without .pub, revoke it and start again — that one is the key itself.

rows: Done. GitHub does not open shells, so the goodbye that follows is normal.
The agent has no key, or GitHub has a different one. Re-run ssh-add.
Are you sure you want to continue connecting?
First contact. Compare the fingerprint with GitHub's published list, then accept.

sections.title: Move repos off HTTPS
sections.summary: A repo cloned over HTTPS keeps asking for a token until you switch it.

items: HTTPS remotes start with https://github.com/.
SSH remotes start with git@github.com:.
New clones: copy the SSH url from the green Code button.

sections.title: Two accounts on one machine
sections.summary: Work and personal cannot share a key — GitHub allows a key on one account only.

blocks.caption: The host alias in the remote url decides which key is used.

items.label: git@github-work:…
items.detail: A made-up host name that exists only in your config and in work remote urls
explain: github-work is not a domain and resolves nowhere. ssh looks it up in ~/.ssh/config, reads the real HostName from that entry, and connects to github.com as usual.
Putting it in the remote url of every work repository makes the choice of key part of the clone, rather than a setting you have to remember to flip.

items.label: git@github.com:…
items.detail: The real host name, left alone so personal repos keep working unchanged
explain: Personal repositories keep the real host name, so they match the default entry in the config and go on using the default key.
Nothing in those clones has to change — which is the reason to alias the work side rather than the other way round.

items.label: ~/.ssh/config
items.detail: Matches the host name in the url, then hands ssh the key named on that entry
explain: One Host block per account: HostName github.com, User git, an IdentityFile pointing at that account's key, and IdentitiesOnly yes.
IdentitiesOnly yes matters more than it looks. Without it, ssh offers every key in the agent, GitHub accepts the first one that works, and you push as the wrong account.

items.label: id_work
items.detail: Uploaded to the work account. GitHub allows one key on one account only
explain: Generate it under its own name — ssh-keygen -f ~/.ssh/id_work — so it never quietly overwrites the key that is already in ~/.ssh.
It is uploaded to the work account and only there. GitHub rejects the same public key on a second account, which is why a second key exists at all.

items.label: id_ed25519
items.detail: Uploaded to the personal account — which is the reason two keys are needed at all
explain: The default key stays exactly where it is and keeps serving the personal account, so nothing that already worked stops working.
Which of the two is used is decided by the host name in the url, never by which key happened to be added to the agent first.

items: IdentitiesOnly yes stops the agent offering every key it holds.
Clone work repos as git@github-work:org/repo.git.
Set user.email per repo too, or commits carry the wrong identity.
